articles.title: Maidstone Christmas trees avoid heatwave growth issues
articles.summary: Kingswood Christmas Trees are unaffected by summer heatwave growth problems, says grower.
articles.body:
A Kent Christmas tree farmer says his crop has bucked the regional trend of poor growth due to the hot summer.

Growers across south-east England have reported stunted pine tree growth, and saplings withering away during the hot summer in which some places did not see rainfall for 40 days.

However Rob Schroeder from Kingswood Christmas Trees near Maidstone said the heatwaves did not particularly affect his stock as it was already well established.

"I think it will be a very good season despite the dry weather. The Nordmann fir are very deep-rooted to reach the moisture in the soil and they look remarkably well, although cost of living issues are making it harder to grow them."

Christmas trees have been grown at the family farm since Schroeder's father first planted them in 1955.

However, despite weathering the extreme climate this year, the farm is feeling the challenges of a tougher financial environment.

"Like all farming and a lot of other businesses it's very challenging," says Schroeder.

"The price of diesel has doubled, fertilisers are up, labour costs are up, so it's a struggle."

Yet Schroeder has made the decision to not raise his prices this year after tracking inflation in 2025 as "things are hard for everybody so we've got to be reasonable".

The farm sells about 5,000 Christmas trees each year with sizes ranging from 3ft (91cm) to those best suited for outdoor displays.

"The biggest ones we do normally are 22 foot [6.7m] but there's quite a few 20-foot [6m] trees - the Port of Dover are having two, the Herne Bay Community Centre and I think even Margate Cemetery - but the most popular is a 6ft [1.8m] Nordmann fir, that goes in the house well," Schroeder says.

Customers are advised to care for their trees to prevent leaf drop by cutting off about half an inch (12mm} of trunk when they are brought home to open up the pores, before placing in a water-holding stand.

"Trees are very thirsty and can drink a pint (0.6l) of water a day," adds Schroeder.

Once the festive season is over, customers are then encouraged to take their trees to a local recycling centre to be chipped.

articles.title: Can the Republican Party survive Trump?
articles.summary: The party faces a battle for its future after the midterms, but Democrats may ultimately determine whether it recovers.
articles.body:
There is a saying in politics: “Every election is fundamentally about the next one.” On November 3, the Republican Party suffered what some have labelled a near “extinction-level” loss in the 2026 midterms. With the results likely to offer an indication of what lies ahead in the next presidential election, what options do Republicans have for 2028? First, we need to understand why this latest “blue tsunami” occurred. The midterms were a rejection of Trump, not an endorsement of the Democrats.

Last Tuesday’s outcome reflected voters holding Trump responsible for economic disaster, huge increases in the cost of living, his failing war on Iran, and his catering to Israel. It is also a condemnation of the Trump family using the Oval Office to enrich themselves and their friends to an unprecedented degree.

Coming into the midterms, voters saw the Trump administration as corrupt and as having abandoned the populist grassroots that had helped him get elected in the first place. A bad economy, failed tariffs, and an unwanted war widened the gap between the MAGA loyalists – who remain loyal to Trump as a political figure – and the America First factions of the Republican Party, which remain loyal to the values that Trump had campaigned on but failed to deliver. It was the separation of these two groups, once seen as interchangeable, that ultimately destroyed the Trump coalition, which had brought Trump and the Republicans to power in Washington.

During the latest midterms, we witnessed many prominent voices in the conservative movement openly oppose Republican leaders. Popular conservatives such as Tucker Carlson and Marjorie Taylor Greene spoke out publicly against several Republican candidates, including Mike Rogers in Michigan and Ken Paxton in Texas. Former Trump supporter Nick Fuentes advocated for months for his followers to vote for Democrats. Their argument was that Trump had betrayed America First principles and could no longer be trusted. Many former grassroots Trump voters who had supported him because of his economic agenda and because he had said that he wanted “no more wars” had suffered greatly due to the increasing cost of living and job losses. In the end, Trump lost support among young voters, Hispanic and Latino voters, Black men, and suburban and independent voters.

These results put the Republican Party at a critical juncture, leaving many to wonder what vision the party will have in 2028. Should they focus more on the post-Trump era, leaving Trump behind, or double down on his original agenda and rebuild his coalition to stay relevant? There are two major forces at play here: Trump himself, as a powerful figure, and the Republican establishment that wants to regain control of the party and stay relevant. Many observers conflate these two forces, while others believe that Trump reinvented the party and became the establishment in the process. Both are wrong. While Trump is still the most powerful person in the Republican Party, and his broader political operation has many hundreds of millions of dollars to support his agenda, he was never the establishment.

The traditional Republican establishment includes institutional donor networks, former party leaders, Reaganite think tanks, and corporate lobbying groups that accepted Trump’s reign while he was delivering on judges and tax cuts, but never truly accepted his populist takeover. The midterm results have given a boost to the more traditional power structures to attempt, again, to “take their party back”. Both are powerful forces with influential bases. The establishment is counting particularly on the fact that the Trump coalition has weakened considerably and will be hard to regenerate. They think Trump is likely to focus his fundraising efforts on himself – in the form of building his presidential library – rather than helping new candidates. On the grassroots side, Republican voters feel betrayed after Trump’s poor handling of the Epstein scandal, unprecedented political profiteering and corruption allegations, and the war on Iran.

Since these midterms were a referendum on how unpopular Trump has become, this leaves the Republican Party with two primary options: rebuild the Trump coalition or prepare themselves for a post-Trump conservative party. The key question now is how Republican candidates can distance themselves from Trump while at the same time attempting to rebuild his winning voter base. Walking this tightrope will mean finding a way to bring MAGA and America First back together again. This may seem like an impossible task in the current political climate, but it is hard to imagine any other winning scenario.

There are many names already in play, with more likely to enter the field within the coming months. Vice President JD Vance seemed to be the heir apparent with the strongest prospects prior to the recent midterms. Vance is powerful in terms of his proximity to Trump and the support he can garner from MAGA and wealthy donors in the tech industry. He also has ties to the America First crowd. Turning Point USA endorsed him publicly a year ago. Tucker Carlson, with his large following, still supports Vance. On the other hand, Vance will have a hard time distancing himself from the Trump administration’s failures on the economy, immigration, and the war on Iran. Vance will have to walk a fine line, criticising Trump enough to distance himself from bad policies while not losing support from the hardcore MAGA base, which is likely to retaliate if it feels left behind. If Vance refuses to criticise Trump altogether, we will likely see a repeat of the Kamala Harris-Joe Biden scenario. One of Vance’s major weaknesses when it comes to electability is that he is not an establishment figure himself. He faced a difficult race for the US Senate in Ohio in 2022. Trump chose him in 2024 as his running mate due to his ties to the tech billionaires and to challenge the Republican establishment. These factors will complicate Vance’s journey within the 2028 field should the establishment start to regain its footing within Republican leadership circles.

The 2028 establishment favourite within the Trump administration is Marco Rubio. It will be easier for Rubio to distance himself from Trump’s economy, but he will have a harder time distancing himself from Trump’s foreign policy and the war. Rubio is well-liked within the establishment, neoconservative and traditional donor groups. However, he is not a MAGA favourite, nor is he seen as an America First choice. Rubio’s main problem is that he is many people’s second choice. Also, his relationship with controversial donors such as Miriam Adelson will be a significant obstacle for him, as will his views on Israeli influence in US politics.

When thinking about 2028, Ron DeSantis, the outgoing governor of Florida, is another strong player. He is positioning himself to lead the Republican Party after leaving office in January. DeSantis is widely credited with the only success that Republicans had in this brutal midterm. He also has close ties to pro-Israel donors in Florida and nationwide. However, his weak performance and failure in running a national campaign against Trump in 2024 have not been forgotten.

Besides these names, the field will likely have many other candidates, some of whom will represent the establishment, and more who will challenge both forces alike. While the midterms were a referendum on Trump’s lack of popularity, they were also a vote against the establishment. Many Republicans and conservatives will pick up on this momentum and attempt to act on it. In this camp, we could see people like Congressman Thomas Massie, a possible run by former Congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene, as well as complete outsiders who we don’t yet know. The determining factor, in my opinion, will be the Democrats. The Democrats’ strategy in managing the next two years will play a major role in the success or failure of the Republicans in 2028. In other words, 2028 is now the Democrats’ to lose.

Whether Democrats focus on anti-Trump retaliation or on rebuilding the economy and regaining voter trust will shape the Republicans’ ability to make a comeback. Retaliation will give Trump another chance at survival, but Democrats will have little incentive to shift their focus to anything other than anti-Trump rhetoric if they insist on keeping their current leadership as it is, without any radical shift against their donor class and wealthy elites.

Last Tuesday was a historic event the likes of which I have not seen in more than a decade on the campaign trail. This victory complicates the Democrats’ path to achieving real success for the American people, especially given Trump’s veto power. More than anything else, the future of the Republican Party will be determined by the ability of the Democrats to come up with their own strategy that is not dependent on being anti-Trump. In some ways, the Democrats need Trump – and need him to keep failing – in order for them to continue this winning streak. It will be up to Republicans to decide on their own whether they need him or not, and whether their party’s future will centre on the personality of one man.

articles.title: Divorced after five days - the story of a 'sham marriage'
articles.summary: Jane, who met her husband on a dating app, says he dropped the bombshell news in a text message.
articles.body:
Five days after her Islamic wedding, Jane received a text message which turned her life upside down.

"I divorce you and have divorced you," wrote her new husband.

Jane - whose real name the BBC has agreed not to publish - said she had met him on the Muslim marriage website Muzz 10 months earlier.

At the time, she believed he was called Adam and that he lived in Manchester.

"It's very hard for me. I thought I was getting into a marriage and instead I got into my worst nightmare," she said.

"It's just crazy. I don't understand why people do this kind of stuff for sex."

Jane said they spent six months chatting online together and on video calls before agreeing to meet in person.

She told the BBC she believed their relationship to be genuine and did not question what was happening when he subsequently proposed.

"He made me believe that he loved me and that he wanted to build a life with me, so I had no reason to really doubt him," she said.

She later discovered Adam's real name was different and that he was already married.

Adam's lawyers said he rejected Jane's allegations in their entirety.

On 2 June, Jane - a convert to Islam - went to Brierfield in Lancashire for a nikah - an Islamic marriage contract or ceremony under Sharia law.

Such contracts, however, are not the same as a civil legal marriage and are not legally recognised as marriage in England and Wales.

Jane said she wanted to get married in her home city of Glasgow, surrounded by friends and family, but said her future husband objected to a wedding in Scotland.

She now looks back on this moment as a warning sign.

"In Scotland, they asked for legal marriage and a nikah to be done at the same time," she explained.

"He said 'Why do they need to see my ID? I mean, nikah is very simple and they don't need to see my ID at all'.

"And so he was really upset about that."

Jane said the ceremony in Brierfield took place in the presence of two imams who acted as witnesses and the couple then spent two nights at a hotel.

Just five days after the wedding, however, Jane received the message informing her that their marriage was over.

Jane said she was left feeling shocked and confused, describing it as a "sham marriage".

Jane believes her "shocking" experience amounted to emotional and sexual exploitation.

The BBC understands he remains married to another woman, both legally and religiously.

In a detailed response through his lawyers, he said the allegations were part of a sustained campaign against him, were unsupported by evidence, and were false.

They told the BBC he had not deceived Jane about his previous marriage because he had not mentioned it.

He had also not hidden his identity during the ceremony with Jane because he provided his driving licence.

The BBC has seen a copy of Jane's Islamic marriage certificate provided to her by the mosque, which contains missing and incorrect details.

Mufti Adeel Zaman, the imam who conducted the ceremony, said the marriage had been between two consenting adults who appeared happy and that he did not consider it his responsibility to ask further questions.

"We are deeply saddened by the circumstances that have arisen," he told the BBC.

"Our intention throughout has been to provide appropriate support and assistance while remaining fair to all parties and limiting our comments to matters of which we have direct knowledge."

He acknowledged that mistakes had been made over checking identification but said he had helped uncover the true identity of the man that Jane had married.

The Lancashire Council of Mosques, which has been involved in mediation following the breakdown of the marriage, said those conducting such ceremonies had a responsibility to carry out appropriate checks.

New Beginnings, a group based in Oldham, Greater Manchester, that provides services to people who have converted to Islam, said it had encountered cases involving people who sought to deceive others within the Muslim community.

"We know about these charlatans in our community, the Muslim community, and people they're out there to deceive," said founder Bilal Brown.

He said relationships or marriages that seem rushed or where extended family are not involved are clear warning signs that all may not be well.

Converts to Islam could be particularly vulnerable in such circumstances, he added.

Saima Afzal, a former assistant police and crime commissioner for Lancashire, told BBC North West Tonight the lack of legal recognition afforded to Islamic marriages could be a problem for some women.

"There is the nikah loophole that you hear about quite a lot around: 'Well, we can't do them for bigamy because nikah is not legally recognised in the UK'," she said.

"Putting that to one side about nikah, let's look at the behaviours here.

"So you've got trickery, manipulation and ensnaring really a woman.

An independent review presented to Parliament in 2018 found that a significant number of Islamic marriages were not followed by civil marriages, leaving people without the protections associated with legally recognised marriages.

Police Scotland said no criminality had been established in Scotland.

Greater Manchester Police confirmed it had been asked to investigate a complaint made by Jane.

Muzz said the man had been permanently blocked from its platform.

Its chief executive Shahzad Younas said: "We ask users to declare if they are married (legally or otherwise).

"If they are we block them from the app during sign-up."

He said the company carried out email, telephone number, device and selfie validation as part of its standard checks, while identity verification was optional.

Profiles indicate which checks have and have not been completed.

Jane said she wanted her case to help prevent other women from experiencing similar situations.

"It's an issue in the community," she added. "If I can help any other vulnerable woman like I was, it's a win."

articles.title: Holiday Meal Payments Bill to face final Stormont hurdle
articles.summary: The new law would would help poorer families with food costs during school holidays.
articles.body:
A proposed law which would help poorer families with food costs during school holidays is to face its final hurdle in the Northern Ireland Assembly on Tuesday.

Some parents and charities have welcomed the Holiday Meal Payments Bill , which was brought forward by Sinn Féin's Danny Baker.

It would create a new payment for families whose children receive free school meals, which would be made outside of term time to help with the cost of food.

But Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) Education Minister Paul Givan has been consistently critical of the legislation, warning it will immediately cost his budget £25m to £30m a year at a time when all departments are struggling financially.

Baker said he was motivated to introduce it by some of his experiences of breakfast clubs and meal schemes in youth work.

"There was a young boy, about the same age of my youngest, around seven years old," he explained.

"He was filling his wee pockets up and we caught on to this.

"To cut a long story short, he was bringing home food for his siblings because there just wasn't enough food in the house."

Baker said all ministers had choices to make and the legislation alone could not solve child poverty, but would act as an "early intervention".

Children are eligible for free school meals if their family's household income is below £15,390 a year.

Northern Ireland is the only UK region without government-funded holiday food support, after the Department of Education (DE) ended its £27-per-fortnight holiday meal grant in 2023 .

Baker's legislation was introduced in the Northern Ireland Assembly in March and has been scrutinised by members of the legislative assembly (MLAs) on a number of occasions over the past nine months.

What have campaigners and charities said?

Community and voluntary groups have been publicly supportive of the bill, with some staging a demonstration at Stormont on Monday in a bid to urge MLAs to get it over the finish line.

Louise McCullough, a mum-of-three from east Belfast, was among those who spoke at the event.

She said her children receive free school meals and that she would be directly affected by the legislation.

"There are so many working families who need this, it will change their lives and be massively impactful," she told BBC News NI.

"I can't afford to work full time because of the cost of childcare, and the cost of living.

"We have to do what we can and schemes like free school meals make a difference but so much more needs done... if you can't find money for hungry children what are you doing?

"Our government should be scaffolding our families properly."

Edel Diamond from the South West Belfast Foodbank said organisations like hers had been "filling in the gaps" to help struggling families.

"We shouldn't have to - it's incumbent on our executive to put these initiatives forward," she said.

"This will make such a difference to families we're seeing daily."

Paul Givan said his department does not have enough money to cover meal costs outside of school terms.

Speaking to the BBC's Good Morning Ulster programme ahead of the vote, he warned other education services would have to be cut to fund meal payments.

"The problem with [Baker's] private member's bill is that this funding doesn't come from the Department of Finance," Givan said.

"It is a Sinn Féin private member's bill with a Sinn Féin finance minister that are literally picking the pocket of the Department for Education to pay a welfare payment."

He warned it will "require an annual commitment of nearly £25m to £30m" and challenged supporters to identify which services they would cut to pay for it.

"To take the funding out of special educational needs and maintenance programmes in schools in order to make a welfare payment to people that are entitled to free school meals is not a responsible decision," Givan added.

Last month, his department tabled amendments that would have given him power to delay its implementation, but these were rejected by a majority of parties .

Ulster Unionist leader Jon Burrows said his party would not support the bill, saying that it was "undermining" the executive's case for asking London for additional funding to solve its budget impasse.

Although the DUP and UUP are set to vote against the bill on Tuesday, Sinn Féin is expected to have enough support from Alliance and SDLP MLAs to ensure the bill passes.

articles.title: Northallerton twin sisters 'ran for our lives' as Krakow attack unfolded
articles.summary: Sienna and Rimini Chapman were in Poland celebrating a friend's birthday when the attack happened.
articles.body:
Twin sisters who were in Krakow when a gunman killed six people have told how they "ran for our lives" when they heard shots.

Sienna and Rimini Chapman, 20, from Northallerton, North Yorkshire, were part of a group celebrating a friend's 21st birthday in Poland when gunfire sounded in the city's Main Market Square at about 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) on Saturday.

The 24-year-old attacker, who died in hospital on Monday, fatally shot four Polish citizens, a British national and an Austrian woman, while a further 15 people, including two police officers, were injured.

Sienna told the BBC their experiences during the attack had been "terrifying".

The group of friends were walking towards a cafe in the square when they first heard gunfire.

"At first I thought the shots were to scare the pigeons away, but then everyone suddenly started running towards us," Sienna said.

"We realised something was wrong and ran in the opposite direction for our lives."

Rimini described the scene as "manic", with the group finding a cafe down a side street where they were ushered in by American tourists who had also heard the shots.

Staff and other customers inside the cafe had not heard gunfire and were "carrying on as normal", Rimini said.

She added: "Everyone else was completely oblivious. It was like we were in two different worlds where we had heard the shots but other people weren't aware.

"We were telling the staff to lock the doors, but I don't think they understood what we were saying because of the language barrier.

"After a few minutes though they did lock the doors."

The sisters, originally from Worcester, said they took shelter under tables and stayed there for two hours while keeping in touch with family members and following BBC News updates about the attack online.

Sienna added: "We eventually felt safe enough to leave and return to our nearby hotel, where we stayed for the rest of the evening.

"The whole experience was terrifying, we were extremely shaken by what had happened."

Rimini said the group had initially planned to have a meal out to celebrate Millie's birthday on Saturday evening but later focused on returning to the UK following the attack.

"We were all a bit fearful and we thought, how can we celebrate when we know people have died?

"We just sat and spoke about the whole thing. I still haven't been able to comprehend it."

In addition to the six people killed in central Krakow, police found the bodies of the gunman's parents and sister at his address on Saturday.

In the hours after the shooting, a Polish government minister said early investigations indicated the attacker was inspired by "far-right ideologies".

On Monday, the country's Prosecutor Office said the investigation into his motive remained ongoing.

articles.title: Rare flowers rescued from eroded coastline at Culbin Sands
articles.summary: The tiny one-flowered wintergreens were rescued from an area of eroded coastline at Culbin Sands.
articles.body:
Conservationists say thousands of rare flowers have been saved from falling into the sea on the Moray coast.

In the UK, the one-flowered wintergreen can only be found in pine woodlands in north-east Scotland.

More than half the entire population of the star-shaped flower have been lost over the last 50 years.

About 3,400 of the tiny plants have been rescued from an area of eroded beach at Culbin Sands, an area of dunes and forest near Findhorn, and moved to a safe location nearby.

More stories from North East Scotland, Orkney and Shetland

Listen to news from North East Scotland on BBC Sounds

Plantlife Scotland worked with Forestry and Land Scotland, NatureScot and volunteers to rescue the plants.

A patch of the flowers was carefully dug up at a site on the coast where it has been eroded away by the sea over the last few years.

Sam Jones, senior ecological adviser at Plantlife Scotland, said: "This type of ground-breaking conservation work will help ensure endangered species like the one-flowered wintergreen are not lost.

"It has been a privilege to be able to help save this patch of the precious and rare one-flowered wintergreen which was at serious risk of being lost."

The plant is often found growing in fungi-rich areas.

Instead of relying on photosynthesis - a process involving sunlight, water and carbon dioxide - to create food and oxygen to survive, the flowers can also take energy from fungus in woodland soils.

Conservationists said increasingly warmer conditions caused by climate change risked drying up these damp soils.

Iain Macdonald, biodiversity adviser at NatureScot said: "We don't yet know how many plants will survive at their new home in Culbin Forest.

"But we do know that it was only a matter of time before they would have all been lost to the sea if we'd left them where they were.

"So, any survival will be a success, and if we can continue to introduce more plants to some of the small, existing populations then we'll strengthen their ability to cope with our changing environment."

articles.title: Palestine Weekly: West Bank on fire – and Gaza’s tents under water
articles.summary: More than 2,000 Gaza buildings risk collapse amid floods, with 400,000 displaced in vulnerable zones, says government.
articles.body:
The first major storm of the season flooded about 70,000 tents in Gaza within 12 hours, killing at least five people and causing about $3m in damage, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office.

The storm hit over the weekend. By Monday, Gaza’s Civil Defence had logged more than 2,100 distress calls, warning that more than 2,000 buildings risk collapse. Nearly 400,000 displaced people shelter in areas judged highly vulnerable.

Israel is blocking 60,000 mobile homes and 200,000 tents, allowing only 20,000 tents into Gaza, where about 85 percent of homes have been destroyed or damaged by Israel’s three-year genocidal war.

Gaza’s Crossings and Borders Authority said Israel also let in no aid trucks or commercial goods on November 6 and 7; five trucks of cooking gas entered the next day. The UN’s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) says Israel notified the UN on November 1 that it would suspend shipments from Egypt, and aid groups warn daily cooked meals could fall from about 600,000 to 330,000 as a result.

Gaza’s Ministry of Health says 20 more Palestinians were killed over the past week, bringing the toll since the October 2025 “ceasefire” to 1,613 as of November 9. Among them:

Storm collapse, November 8: A sand embankment fell onto tents at a displacement site southwest of Deir el-Balah. Five bodies were recovered, among them Tahrir Nabhan and her daughter Maryam, and Habiba al-Zein.

Strikes and shootings: On November 3, Rimas al-Madhoun, 16, was killed in a strike on a tent in Gaza City. Two days later, Noura Sheikh al-Eid was killed by tank fire in al-Mawasi hours after her daughter left for treatment in Egypt, and 12-year-old Adnan al-Qirnawi was shot and killed east of Bureij the same day. Nermin al-Amour and Mahmoud Abu Hammad were then killed on November 8 in a Khan Younis strike.

The weekend storm came as Hamas urged mediators and the Board of Peace not to link reconstruction to political or security conditions.

Arab-led parties at the table, and in the crosshairs

The political battle over Gaza’s future is unfolding as parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel hold potentially decisive leverage in Israel’s post-election negotiations – amid an ongoing demonisation campaign against the parties and Arab voting power in Israel.

President Isaac Herzog gave opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot the mandate to form a government over the weekend after 67 members of parliament recommended him , against 46 for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Eisenkot wants a “national emergency government” open to any party accepting four principles, including recognition of Israel as a “Jewish and democratic” state, and Hamas as a “terrorist” group to be destroyed. For his part, Netanyahu gave a speech seeking a “national unity” government with Eisenkot, Likud, and his Haredi and far-right allies, warning that a government reliant on Arab-led parties would be backed by those who “want to eliminate Israel”.

One of the Arab-led blocs, the Joint List, has said its priority is to topple the Netanyahu government, but that it cannot join an administration that violates international law. It has also said it expects action on education, welfare and crime if it is to support Eisenkot from outside government.

In discussions with Herzog, Mansour Abbas, the leader of the other Arab-led party, the United Arab List (Ra’am), declined to call Hamas a “terror” group, citing fear for his family, while backing its disarmament, according to the Times of Israel. Avigdor Liberman, leader of the opposition Yisrael Beytenu party, repeated that no government should rely on either Palestinian-led party.

Beyond the rhetoric, journalist Abed Abou Shhadeh, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, was released without charge on November 8 after five days in the custody of the domestic intelligence agency, the Shin Bet, saying his arrest was meant “to intimidate Arab society as a whole”.

The Shin Bet chief sought to question leaders of the Palestinian-led parties, but Israel’s attorney general says the fraud probes would not “even remotely” change the result of the election. Tensions on the streets led to a far-right march through a Palestinian neighbourhood in the mixed city of al-Lyd (Lod) on the evening of November 8, which ended in a brawl and 11 arrests, according to the Times of Israel.

West Bank: Takeovers, seizures and a harvest under attack

On November 4, about 30 settlers backed by the settler group Nachala entered Ein a-Duyuk a-Tahta, near Jericho, and took over eight Palestinian homes. Peace Now, citing reports, said settlers shot a Palestinian man in the leg, and the UN said the army declared a closed military zone, blocking humanitarian access.

Settlers say they bought the homes through Nachala; Jericho Governor Hussein Hamayel called the sale a forgery.

For months , the state has backed settlers’ land razing and takeover efforts in the area, and that continued this week. The Jerusalem Post reported the alleged purchase was coordinated with the settler Binyamin Regional Council.

Haaretz reported that Central Command chief Major General Avi Bluth knew of the entry in advance and told the settlers not to alert senior officers until they were inside, with three army platoons diverted to protect the settlers during the takeover of houses; the army called the Haaretz report false.

But Jericho was only the most dramatic case of a multi-pronged escalation in which land seizures, demolitions, attacks and arrests unfolded in the West Bank, with settlers, soldiers and the Civil Administration often working in concert.

Attacks on the olive harvest: OCHA counts 377 harvest-related attacks since September 1, more than any previous season. In October alone, OCHA documented 457 attacks causing casualties or damage in the West Bank, the most in any month since it began counting in 2006. In Burqa, northwest of Ramallah, settlers set olive groves on fire on November 5 while forces stopped residents from putting them out. Near Salfit, settlers beat three young men with clubs on November 8, and on November 9 they drove farmers off land near Silwad and injured one near Tayasir, according to Palestinian state news agency Wafa.

Demolitions: On November 4, forces demolished 21 structures belonging to three families in the northern Jordan Valley and five homes in Biddu the next day. On November 9, according to Wafa, a 200-square-metre house, its well and fruit trees were razed in al-Hijra, near Dura.

Sieges and closures: Settlers entered the sixth week of a nearly complete siege of Yusuf Shanaran’s home in Wadi al-Rakheem, according to Shanaran. According to village mayor Marwan Sabah, a similar settler siege continues of the Abayet family home in Umm Safa, which recently received demolition orders from the Israeli Civil Administration, despite it being built before Israel’s occupation began in 1967. In the south, forces closed Hebron’s Ibrahimi Mosque to Palestinians for two days during a Jewish holiday, days after the army ended a 10-day operation in the city.

articles.title: US citizen shot by ICE officer near school bus stop sues Trump administration for $25m
articles.summary: A US citizen who was shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in the country’s southern California has filed a $25 million lawsuit
articles.body: A US citizen who was shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in the country’s southern California has filed a $25 million lawsuit against the federal government, accusing authorities of using excessive force, wrongfully arresting him and pursuing a case based on fabricated allegations.Carlos Jimenez was reportedly driving to work at a food pantry on October 30, 2025, when he encountered ICE officers conducting an operation in his neighbourhood. According to the complaint filed in federal court on Friday, Jimenez approached the officers around 7 am to warn them that children would soon be arriving at a nearby bus stop.According to the Guardian, the lawsuit alleges that an ICE officer, later identified as Eusebio Ortiz, pointed a gun at Jimenez's face, abused him verbally and threatened to shoot if he did not leave. The complaint cites audio recorded over the officer's radio.Jimenez then claimed to comply and attempted a three-point turn because officers' vehicles were blocking his way. However, Ortiz allegedly fired several shots into the car without warning, hitting Jimenez in the back and right shoulder.The complaint says no officer was in the vehicle's path when the shots were fired and alleges there was no reasonable suspicion or probable cause to stop, threaten or shoot Jimenez.The department of homeland security (DHS) had said at the time that Jimenez attempted to run over officers by reversing towards them without stopping. It described the officer's gunfire as “defensive” shots.Later, the justice department charged Jimenez with assaulting a federal officer using a deadly or dangerous weapon. The federal complaint alleged that he had “rapidly accelerated in reverse” towards an officer.According to the Guardian, the justice department's Los Angeles office has prosecuted 113 people for alleged offences against immigration officers since last spring. A Guardian review found that, as of mid-September, charges against 33 of them had been dismissed and nine others had been acquitted by juries.Jimenez's lawsuit describes the criminal allegations as “fabricated”. It also points out that, despite DHS's claim that the shooting was defensive, the criminal complaint did not include a statement from Ortiz saying he had felt threatened.Lawsuit alleges FBI interfered with medical treatmentThe complaint further alleges that FBI agents followed Jimenez to the hospital and interfered with his medical care, including by pulling a nurse away and preventing him from speaking to medical staff.According to the lawsuit, agents removed him from his hospital bed, placed him in a waist restraint and took him back to the shooting site for questioning while a bullet was still lodged in his body.As per the complaint, Jimenez was bleeding and vomiting in the agents' van when officers told him not to “ruin their vehicle”.The lawsuit also accuses the FBI of falsely claiming that two neighbours witnessed the incident and told an agent that Jimenez had enough room to drive forward rather than reverse.However, Jimenez's lawyers allege that both witnesses denied making those statements when interviewed by the defence. They also said they had not known about the shooting until they saw reports about it in the media, according to the complaint.During the criminal proceedings, defence lawyers sought access to officers' text messages. A judge ordered the government to produce records of agents' communications in May, The Guardian reported.Prosecutors subsequently agreed to resolve the case through a diversion agreement, under which the charges could be dropped at the end of October if Jimenez met certain conditions. The lawsuit alleges that prosecutors sought to avoid the disclosure of communications and the questioning of an FBI agent accused of fabricating witness statements.The criminal charges were formally dismissed last week.Jimenez seeks more than $25 million in damagesThe lawsuit seeks more than $25 million in damages, including compensation for lost wages and medical expenses. It alleges excessive force, assault, false arrest and other violations, and says Jimenez still has bullet fragments lodged near his lung.Justice department spokesperson Ciaran McEvoy did not comment on the lawsuit but said Jimenez “could have exercised his right to take the case to trial, but he instead requested that our office agree to resolve the case through a diversion agreement”.The case bears similarities to that of Francisco Longoria, another southern California resident who was shot by an ICE officer during a traffic stop last year and later faced criminal charges that were dropped.You use AI every day. articles.title: China’s trade surplus surpasses $1 trillion for a 2nd straight year, as exports surge 35%
articles.summary: China’s trade surplus exceeded $1 trillion for a second straight year, according to official data released Tuesday, as pressure mounts for greater balance in trade with Beijing.
articles.body: HONG KONG — China’s trade surplus exceeded $1 trillion for a second straight year, according to official data released Tuesday, as pressure mounts for greater balance in trade with Beijing. Exports in October surged 35.2% from a year earlier, the customs agency said. Exports have grown rapidly this year, supported by high-tech goods like semiconductors and autos. Imports rose 41.6% year-on-year. From January to October, China logged a $1.04 trillion trade surplus, even as the trade surplus narrowed last month to $105.3 billion from $133.5bn in September as imports picked up pace. That puts China on track to surpass last year’s record surplus of $1.2 trillion. “We expect Chinese exports to stay strong for the rest of this year, led by electronics and autos,” said Dave Chia, an economist at Moody’s Analytics. China’s imports soared in October partly because of a recovery in shipments of crude oil from the Persian Gulf. Overcapacity in many industries, excess domestic savings and weakened domestic demand are still leading China to ship its goods abroad as some countries move to protect their own industries, said Alicia García-Herrero, chief economist for Asia Pacific at French bank Natixis. The situation is not sustainable, she said. Businesses are feeling the pressure of ferocious competition as China’s economy has slowed, said Cinders Zhou, who sells eyewear for a manufacturer in the city of Linhai in eastern China’s Zhejiang province. “It comes down to product quality, or rather the increasing lack of it across the industry, since there’s significant homogenization,” said Zhou, whose company makes frames and lenses sold both in and outside China. “That has forced everyone to compete on price,” she said. Trade curbs by the European Union pose an important risk at a time of heightened U.S. trade barriers and tariffs, Chia said. Still, the E.U.’s trade measures apply to only a small part of China’s exports, said Nguyen Hoang Nam from Capital Economics. China has insisted it is not seeking to expand its surplus but wants more balanced global trade. However, strong exports have helped offset sluggish domestic demand. The economy is forecast to meet Beijing’s official target of a 4.5% to 5% annual growth this year, slightly slower than last year’s 5% expansion. China’s exports to the U.S. grew 32.9% in October year-on-year, building on a low base after China-U.S. trade was hit last year by Trump’s elevated tariffs. China’s exports to the E.U. in October rose 24.3% year-on-year. They rose 17.2% in January-October. For the first ten months, the trade surplus with the U.S. was around $266.5 billion, while for the E.U., the 10-month difference was more than $310 billion. In 2025, the E.U. recorded a roughly $410 billion trade deficit with China, or more than $1.1 billion each day. Figures reported by China often differ from those reported by its trading partner. Also in October, China’s semiconductor exports soared 137.1% in terms of value from the year before. Exports of autos rose 37.6%. China’s exports could be vulnerable to setbacks for the artificial intelligence industry, a concern that deepened with the Democratic victories in the U.S. midterm elections given the public backlash against expansion of data centers. “If the AI boom slows or turns into a correction, lower chip and electronics prices and smaller shipping volumes would hit China’s exports hard,” Chia said. Trade is likely to be among the top issues on the agenda in planned meetings between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping next week on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders summit in the Chinese technology hub of Shenzhen. A two-month extension of a trade truce until January has provided some relief to exporters, though it’s unclear how long that may last. U.S. and European trade policies have added “a lot of difficulties” for Chinese businesses to expand in the markets, said Wang Xin, head of the Shenzhen Cross-Border E-Commerce Association, an industry group.

articles.title: A fake GoFundMe collected $17,750 after 67 people died in a Washington plane crash; a Russian lawyer spotted suspicious emails and helped get the campaign removed
articles.summary: A fraudulent GoFundMe campaign claiming to raise money for the family of two victims of the January 2025 Washington plane crash collected $17,750 before
articles.body: A fraudulent GoFundMe campaign claiming to raise money for the family of two victims of the January 2025 Washington plane crash collected $17,750 before being taken down, after a Russian lawyer identified suspicious activity and alerted the fundraising platform. The campaign, which had a target of $150,000, claimed to support the family of Kansas farmers Bob and Lori Schrock, who were among the 67 people killed when an American Eagle passenger aircraft collided with a US Army helicopter near Washington, DC. Gauthier Daniel Igorevich, a Moscow-based criminal lawyer, became suspicious after contacting the person listed as the fundraiser's representative. His investigation revealed unusual email exchanges, including a request for a $15,000 transfer to a Skrill account.Fake fundraiser claimed to support family of Kansas farmersThe GoFundMe campaign appeared after the January 29, 2025, collision involving American Eagle Flight 5342 and a US Army Black Hawk helicopter near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport. All 64 people aboard the passenger aircraft and all three helicopter crew members died.Among the victims were Bob and Lori Schrock, a farming couple from Kiowa, Kansas. They operated a canola and wheat farming business and were travelling from Wichita to Washington when the collision occurred.The fundraiser claimed to collect donations for the Schrock family and set a target of $150,000. It listed a contact named "Sam Lorri Otim", supposedly from Kiowa, Kansas. However, when DTN investigated the campaign, it could not find anyone by that name living in the town, and the listed contact did not respond to the publication's enquiries.Russian lawyer noticed suspicious details in email exchangeGauthier Daniel Igorevich, a Moscow-based criminal lawyer with Trunov, Ayvar and Partners, came across the fundraiser while researching a potential legal case connected to the plane crash. He was representing families of Russian citizens who had died in the collision, including relatives of former Russian-born figure skating world champions Yevgenia Shishkova and Vadim Naumov.After finding the campaign, Igorevich contacted the listed representative to offer legal assistance to the Schrock family. However, the responses raised concerns. The person communicating with him did not provide a name and referred to themselves only as a "family representative".Igorevich also found that the photographs used on the fundraising page were publicly available. He told DTN that these details made him question whether the campaign was genuinely connected to the victims' family.Alleged $15,000 payment request raised further concernsThe email exchange became more suspicious when the person claiming to represent the family allegedly asked Igorevich to transfer $15,000 to a Skrill account simply for his law firm to be considered for legal representation.The representative also claimed that the family had already spent $15,000 trying to secure the services of another law firm. Igorevich responded that his firm would reimburse the family for that amount.However, the person continued to insist that he send the money to the specified Skrill account before the firm could be given the legal work. The exchange strengthened the lawyer's suspicion that someone was attempting to exploit the crash for financial gain."I couldn't just sit back. I had to report it," Igorevich told DTN, explaining why he decided to alert GoFundMe.GoFundMe removes campaign and refunds donorsIgorevich reported the suspicious correspondence to GoFundMe and shared details of his interaction with the campaign's representative. He also contacted DTN journalist Todd Neeley, who investigated the fundraiser, checked the identity listed on its page and reviewed copies of the emails.By the time the campaign was removed on Monday afternoon, it had reportedly collected $17,750 towards its $150,000 target. The largest reported individual donation was $10,500, while another contribution was approximately $5,000.A GoFundMe spokesperson told DTN that the platform had removed the fundraiser, refunded donors and banned the account responsible from creating future campaigns. The company said it refunded $17,550, a figure that differs by $200 from the $17,750 reported as raised when the campaign was taken down.GoFundMe also confirmed that the organiser had never gained access to the donations because the money was being held securely by its payment processors.GoFundMe directs donors to verified crash-related fundraisersFollowing the incident, GoFundMe highlighted a centralised fundraising hub containing campaigns verified by its Trust and Safety team for people affected by the Washington plane crash.The platform said the hub was intended to make it easier for people to identify legitimate ways to support victims, their families and others affected by the collision. The incident also demonstrated how fraudulent fundraisers can exploit publicly available photographs and information about victims to make campaigns appear genuine.The FBI had separately warned in January 2025 about charitable fraud linked to mass-casualty incidents and disasters, advising people to verify fundraising campaigns and check whether donations are reaching their stated beneficiaries.You use AI every day. articles.title: US moves aircraft from second UK base over ‘threat from Iran’
articles.summary: Two refuelling tankers and several other aircraft diverted from RAF Mildenhall airbase to other locations, WSJ reports.
articles.body:
The United States military has moved aircraft from a second ⁠airbase in the United Kingdom “in the wake of a threat from Iran”, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

Two US refuelling tankers and several other tankers that were using the RAF Mildenhall military base in eastern England diverted to Germany and other locations on Monday, the WSJ reported on Tuesday.

The report said the precise nature of the threat to RAF Mildenhall remains under discussion among US officials.

The US upgraded the security posture at RAF Mildenhall and RAF Lakenheath to Force Protection Condition (FPCON) Charlie, the WSJ report said, quoting a US official familiar with ‌the matter.

FPCON Charlie is the second-highest defensive threat level in the US Department of Defense’s security system and occurs when intelligence indicates that a form of “terrorist” action is likely.

“We do not routinely comment on the activity of other nations,” a UK Ministry of Defence spokesperson said in a statement.

“Aircraft and other assets move regularly according to operational requirements.”

A US Air Force spokesperson said aircraft rotate ⁠between installations and operating locations for various reasons.

The report comes weeks after five men were arrested outside RAF Fairford airbase in southwest England over a security incident, with two others arrested later on suspicion of assisting Iranian intelligence.

The circumstances of the September incident remain largely unexplained, but it prompted the US to remove its B-1 bombers from the airbase on security grounds.

It came at a time of heightened concern about the ⁠wider security implications of the US-Israel war on Iran.

RAF Fairford had been used by US bombers that carried out strikes on ‌Iran.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last month that the activity at RAF Fairford was likely to have been coordinated in Iran.

While Tehran’s ambassador to the UK has denied accusations that it was involved in ‌any ‌plot against the airbase, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said in July that Fairford and any other base used to launch attacks against Iran were legitimate targets.

articles.title: California voters reject billionaire tax
articles.summary: The proposed measure would have imposed a one-time 5 percent tax on Californian billionaires to fund healthcare.
articles.body:
Voters in California have rejected a proposed tax on billionaires, according to projections by the Associated Press news agency.

With about 60 percent of votes counted, the tax proposal appeared to be headed for defeat on Tuesday, with the “no” vote leading at 55.6 percent compared with 44.4 percent for “yes”.

The measure would impose a one-time 5 percent tax on Californians whose net worth exceeds $1bn.

Known as Proposition 40, the tax would have raised $100bn, most of which would have been earmarked for healthcare programmes, but education and food-assistance programmes would also receive funds.

It was championed by United States Senator Bernie Sanders and other progressive politicians as a remedy for economic inequality and a model for the rest of the country.

Democrats said the tax was necessary to offset federal funding cuts in President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill.

However, outgoing California Governor Gavin Newsom, a likely candidate for the 2028 Democratic Party presidential nomination, came out against the measure.

Newsom and other opponents to Proposition 40 argued it would prompt ultrawealthy and high-tech entrepreneurs to leave California, taking their income-tax payments and job-producing enterprises with them.

Newsom’s opposition, as well as division among party leaders and labour unions, led initial support for the measure to wane ahead ⁠of the vote, which was held during the midterm elections.

Californian billionaires , including Google cofounder Sergey Brin, spent more than a quarter of a billion dollars campaigning against the measure, arguing it was a gateway to more aggressive taxation for all Californians and could target their retirement accounts.

The failure to pass the tax is a blow to the Democratic Party’s left wing, which has gained momentum after a so-called “blue tsunami” in the country’s midterm elections saw Democrats winning majorities in both chambers of the US Congress.

Incoming US Senate Finance Committee Chairman Ron Wyden has signalled, however, that taxing the ultrawealthy remains a central goal for the Democratic Party as a whole.

“The committee will redouble ‌its ‌efforts to ensure billionaires pay their fair share and hold tax cheats accountable,” he said in a November 4 statement outlining the panel’s priorities.

articles.title: Troy Lotspeich’s great-grandfather bought their ranch in northern Oklahoma in 1903; today the family rotates 600 cow-calf pairs through 25 paddocks on 10,000 acres of native grass, winning landowner of the year
articles.summary: A ranch in northwestern Oklahoma has remained in one family for more than a century, but its latest distinction comes from how the land is being managed.
articles.body: A ranch in northwestern Oklahoma has remained in one family for more than a century, but its latest distinction comes from how the land is being managed. Troy Lotspeich’s great-grandfather bought the family's current ranch in 1903. Today, the 10,000-acre property is home to 600 cattle that are moved through 25 grazing paddocks, giving native grasslands time to recover while supporting a diverse population of wildlife. The Oklahoma Department of Wildlife Conservation (ODWC) has now named the Lotspeich family its 2026 Landowner Conservationist of the Year.The award, announced on October 12, recognises the family's efforts to balance cattle production with wildlife habitat conservation. According to the department, the main Lotspeich Ranch in northern Harper County comprises native grasses, forbs and shrubs. The family also owns an additional 3,950 acres of farmland in Beaver County, including 750 acres of irrigated land.The ranch's history stretches back to the 1890s, when Lotspeich's great-grandfather first arrived in Oklahoma and purchased a quarter-section of land. He subsequently bought the property that became the family's current ranch in 1903. Generations later, the land continues to support a working cattle operation, but its management has increasingly focused on maintaining the prairie ecosystem.How 25 paddocks help protect the grasslandThe family follows a rotational grazing system in which its 600 cattle are moved through 25 paddocks across the 10,000-acre ranch during the growing season. Instead of allowing livestock to graze continuously across the same stretch of land, the approach concentrates grazing in one area for a shorter period before cattle are moved elsewhere. The system follows a principle known as "take half, leave half", which means leaving enough grass behind for vegetation to recover and continue providing food and shelter for wildlife. The department describes the approach as high-intensity, low-duration grazing. It can improve soil conditions and organic matter, helping the ground absorb and retain more rainwater.Water availability is particularly important in this part of Oklahoma. The region receives an average of only around 22 inches of precipitation annually, making it essential to conserve moisture and allow native vegetation to recover between grazing periods. To make the system work across the property, the family has installed approximately 35 miles of water lines connected to 20 stock tanks. These provide at least one water source for each paddock, reducing the need for cattle to travel long distances to drink. Troy also monitors grazing pressure through structures called grazing exclosures, which allow him to compare vegetation in protected areas with grass exposed to livestock.During winter, the cattle are moved away from the native grassland and onto the family's crop ground. There, they graze on wheat pasture supplemented with alfalfa hay or grain produced on the irrigated farmland.A prairie ecosystem shared with wildlifeThe ranch's conservation work has helped sustain a range of wildlife species, including northern bobwhite quail, white-tailed deer, mule deer, elk, prairie dogs, burrowing owls, ring-necked pheasants and wild turkeys. Ducks, geese and sandhill cranes also use the property's ponds and river.Native grasses and forbs play an important role in maintaining this habitat. They provide food and cover for wildlife, while healthy vegetation helps protect soil and retain rainfall. Allowing grasslands time to recover after grazing also helps maintain the varied plant growth that supports different species. Fire is another part of the landscape's natural history. According to ODWC, wildfires have helped shape the vegetation on the ranch. Native prairie plants are adapted to fire and can continue growing even when rainfall is limited. Fire also helps maintain an ecosystem that historically evolved with periodic burning.The family also allows guided hunts for northern bobwhite and white-tailed deer, while youth hunts are organised on the ranch. The Lotspeiches raise and train their own bird dogs, maintaining a connection between the family's ranching traditions and outdoor activities.A family legacy that has changed with the landThe family's relationship with wildlife has evolved over generations. An account from a 1965 edition of Oklahoma Wildlife magazine quoted Troy's grandfather, Kenny Lotspeich, recalling that the ranch once displayed "no hunting" signs. He later decided to remove them, explaining that the signs were keeping genuine friends away while failing to stop poachers from taking birds.Today, the family works closely with the Oklahoma Department of Wildlife Conservation, the Natural Resources Conservation Service and the Farm Service Agency. Troy is also associated with conservation organisations including Pheasants Forever/Quail Forever and the National Wild Turkey Federation. He participates in a Candidate Conservation Agreement with Assurances programme for lesser prairie-chickens, a species whose grassland habitat has faced pressure across parts of the Great Plains.The family's recognition also highlights the importance of private landowners in wildlife conservation in Oklahoma. More than 95% of the state is privately owned, according to the wildlife department, making cooperation with farmers and ranchers important for protecting habitats beyond public conservation areas.You use AI every day. articles.title: Police officer dies and another injured after backpack explosion in Oviedo
articles.summary: Officers attended the scene in connection with a separate incident at a residential building in the city.
articles.body:
A police officer has died and another has been injured in the northern Spanish city of Oviedo after an explosive device went off at the scene of a shooting.

The blast happened when officers from Spain's canine unit and explosives disposal unit arrived and examined a suspicious backpack following reports of a dispute between neighbours on Tuesday morning .

A woman who had been shot and the injured officer have been taken to hospital for treatment.

The suspect fled the scene and is still at large, police said.

Spanish police paid tribute to the dead officer, who has been named as Juan José, in a statement on X and said: "Our hearts are with his family, friends, colleagues and loved ones."

Officers attended the scene early after receiving reports of an argument between neighbours and upon arriving found a woman who had sustained gunshot wounds, police spokesman Pedro Aguado said.

While searching for the suspected attacker, officers found a suspicious backpack with a flashing light and contacted both the bomb disposal unit and canine unit.

"While the package was being moved outside to ensure the safety of the residents, an explosion occurred," Aguado added.

The explosion left a member of the canine unit dead and an officer from the bomb disposal unit seriously injured, he said.

A three-year-old police dog named Deny was also killed in the explosion.

A widespread police operation is ongoing near the scene of the explosion and officers are continuing to hunt for the suspect.

Taking to social media, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he was "deeply shocked" by the fatal incident and paid tribute to the officer injured in the explosion.

"Your dedication and courage deserve the gratitude of an entire country," he said.

Spanish opposition leader and President of the People's Party Alberto Núñez Feijóo said: "What happened in Oviedo is heartbreaking.

"My condolences to the family of the officer who died and my best wishes for the recovery of the one who was seriously injured.

articles.title: Meghan makes first public appearance since father was charged, but pulls out of speech on child safety
articles.summary: Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, canceled plans to address a European Parliament gathering on Tuesday, as the wife of Britain’s Prince Harry made her first public appearance since her father was charged with possessing child sexual abuse photos.
articles.body: Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, canceled plans to address a European Parliament gathering on Tuesday, as the wife of Britain’s Prince Harry made her first public appearance since her father was charged with possessing child sexual abuse photos. The couple appeared at an event to discuss child online safety in Brussels, where Harry delivered a speech at the opening of the Lost Screen Memorial, an art installation commemorating children who died as a result of suffering harm on social media. They were met by waiting delegates and a large press pack, with journalists shouting to ask Meghan how she was feeling. Both dressed in black, they made no comment. Meghan had also been due to speak but cancelled her address, a spokesperson for the couple said. The Daily Telegraph reported that Meghan, who said in a statement last month that she was “deeply distressed” at the allegations about her father, did not feel strong enough to speak at the event. U.S. authorities charged Thomas Markle with possession of child sexual abuse photos last week, including photographs of himself with naked underage girls, found in rented storage units in California. The 82-year-old denied the accusations of possessing child sexual abuse material when they came to light, telling the Daily Mail they were untrue and “sick lies.” Both Harry and Meghan have regularly spoken out about online dangers to children and been critical of major tech companies for not doing more to protect them. The prince made no reference to his father-in-law in his address in Brussels, where the couple opened the Lost Screen Memorial, which they initially launched in New York last year through their charitable organization Archewell. “How did we reach a point where we can build technology capable of extraordinary things, yet still struggle to make it safe for a child?” Harry said as he gave a speech alongside parents who had been affected by the issue. “I’m not here as an expert or a politician. I’m here as a father, my wife, as a mother and together, as a couple who stand alongside parents like Sandra, Megan and Sewell — in New York, Los Angeles, Geneva and now Brussels. Parents who never imagined they would have a reason to be in rooms like this,” he said, referring to parents who believe their children died as a result of online harm. Meghan has been estranged from her father since the run-up to her marriage to King Charles’ younger son Harry in 2018. She said in her statement last month that she had known about the allegations against him since 2018 and had prevented him from having contact with her children Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5, to protect them. Their trip to Brussels follows an appearance in Nottingham in October, their first joint appearance since they moved back to live in Britain, having relocated to the United States in 2020 when they stepped back from official royal duties.

articles.title: Skydance Games cuts jobs a month after Warner Bros merger; company says: This is not a reflection of...
articles.summary: Skydance Games has cut jobs barely a month after its parent company closed its $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery.
articles.body: Skydance Games has cut jobs barely a month after its parent company closed its $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery. The gaming division is among the first parts of the newly merged entertainment giant to be trimmed, with developers across art, design, engineering and writing affected over the last few days.A Skydance spokesperson said the company had stepped back to rethink where it invests its efforts and decided to scale down some of its projects. "As a result, there are roles impacted," the spokesperson said, adding that the cuts did not reflect the talent or creativity of those leaving. The company hasn't shared how many jobs were lost or which projects are being pared back, though reports put the number at 30 or more.Skydance Interactive and Paramount Games staff bear the brunt of the layoffsThe cuts appear to have landed on staff who came from Skydance Interactive, the studio behind The Walking Dead: Saints & Sinners, and Paramount Games. Warner Bros. Games employees do not seem to be part of this round.Rebecca Vessal, a senior gameplay and game AI programmer who kept her job, wrote on LinkedIn that "most of my game team at Skydance Interactive got laid off today." Engineer David Vera, also unaffected, posted that Skydance "just lost a ton of great talent yesterday" and stressed that nobody was let go over performance, before sharing a long list of former colleagues open to new roles.Skydance and Paramount merged their gaming businesses in the summer to form Paramount Games Studio, whose slate includes Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Last Ronin and Avatar Legends: The Fighting Game. Once the Warner deal closed on October 6, it was combined with Warner's in-house developers, including Avalanche Software, NetherRealm, Rocksteady and TT Games, under the Skydance Games banner. Tony Driscoll, who previously oversaw Fortnite's creator economy at Epic Games, heads the group as president of games and experiences.Skydance has promised Wall Street at least $6 billion in merger savingsThe layoffs coincide with co-CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz presenting their first quarterly results since the deal on Monday. The pair have committed to at least $6 billion in cost synergies and have said layoffs will be part of that. Late in October, the company also brought in a five-day office mandate and a voluntary buyout programme.Gaming has barely featured in the merger conversation. When leadership has brought it up, the focus has been on big names, with Ellison and Kreiz pointing to Hogwarts Legacy and Mortal Kombat in an October memo, and Driscoll highlighting Batman.The wider industry isn't offering much cushion either. Microsoft offered voluntary buyouts to a quarter of its workforce last month, Xbox staff included. articles.title: Keeping the edge sharp: India looks to build a global military MRO hub
articles.summary: Combat readiness and effectiveness depend on a multitude of factors.
articles.body: Combat readiness and effectiveness depend on a multitude of factors. One of the most important aspects of ensuring readiness is to ensure that equipment in service, from pistols to aircraft carriers and everything in between remains serviceable. That is why maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) quietly decides how ready a military really is, and why India is working to do more of it at home. The aim is to keep equipment ready, cut reliance on overseas facilities and eventually service the platforms of other countries as well, trying to take a bigger bite of the USD 180 billion dollar market, which is expected to grow to about USD 300 billion by 2034.Keeping the services readyThe Indian Navy depends on the Indian Naval Ship Maintenance Authority (INSMA), and the Indian Air Force (IAF) on its Base Repair Depots (BRDs). The IAF has also identified about 4,000 lines of spares for indigenisation, a figure it gave in 2021. Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) remains central to this, and its Koraput division has overhauled more than 9,000 engines, according to a Defence Ministry announcement in October 2026.The newer projects reach into more complex areas. GE Aerospace signed a contract with the IAF on April 13, 2026, to help set up an IAF-run depot for the F404-IN20 engines that power the Tejas. On May 6, 2026, MBDA agreed with the IAF to build a capability for mid-life overhaul of MICA missiles. In March 2026, the Ministry of Defence signed a Rs 413-crore contract with Boeing India Defence for depot-level maintenance of the Navy's P-8I fleet.The armoured vehicles nigam limited has recently conducted the ground breaking ceremony for a facility in which both the T-90 and T-72 main battle tanks of the army will be overhauled. The overhauling of these vehicles, will improve the serviceability of the army's armoured punch in a conflict.Looking beyond IndiaThe most important step towards serving foreign operators is the C-130J Super Hercules facility being set up by Tata Advanced Systems and Lockheed Martin, whose groundbreaking was announced on December 8, 2025. It is meant to handle depot-level and heavy maintenance for the IAF and for regional and global C-130 operators. Construction was expected to finish by the end of 2026, with the first aircraft due in early 2027.At sea, the Master Shipyard Repair Agreement signed in April 2023 qualified Larsen & Toubro's Kattupalli shipyard to compete for US Navy voyage-repair work. India has also refitted foreign vessels, including Mauritius Coast Guard Ship Victory and the Myanmar Navy's UMS Miye Theinkhatu.Smaller private firms such as Airbornics Defence & Space Limited (ADSL) are also looking abroad, the defence arm of the JCBL Group, has signed a memorandum of understanding with Nigus Hercules Limited of Nigeria to develop MRO for armoured vehicles, engines and air-defence equipment used by Nigeria's armed forces.The road aheadForeign platforms often need proprietary manuals, diagnostic software, tools and manufacturer authorisation, and governments can restrict access to sensitive systems. India will also face competition from established hubs. The distinction that matters most is between facilities that serve India's own forces, projects built with foreign customers in mind, and contracts actually won from foreign militaries. So far, only a few projects fall in the last category.

articles.title: Who moves first in Iran-US diplomacy?
articles.summary: Breaking the deadlock requires coordinated, verifiable concessions, not demands for one side to act first.
articles.body:
For nearly two decades, one question has haunted Iran-US diplomacy: Who should move first? Since the early 2000s, Washington and Tehran have repeatedly faced the same dilemma: Should Iran limit its nuclear activities before receiving economic relief, or should the United States ease pressure before expecting Iranian concessions? Yet the latest diplomatic crisis suggests that these may no longer be the right questions.

The real challenge is not who moves first. It is whether both sides can move together.

This question has become urgent again amid the latest dispute over the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran has proposed reopening the waterway if Washington meets a series of conditions, including lifting the naval blockade, easing sanctions and providing guarantees against renewed attacks. Tehran argues that negotiations cannot begin under conditions of pressure and confrontation. Washington, however, insists that any renewed diplomatic process must address the nuclear issue from the beginning.

This disagreement represents the central problem of the current negotiations: both sides are demanding confidence-building measures before taking the first step. History shows that this dilemma has been addressed before through mechanisms based on reciprocal action.

The 2013 Joint Plan of Action between Iran and the P5+1 – the five permanent United Nations Security Council members and Germany – was built around an interim approach in which both sides accepted limited and reversible measures. Iran agreed to restrictions on parts of its nuclear programme, including limits on enrichment levels and enhanced monitoring, while the US and its partners provided limited sanctions relief.

This approach later evolved into the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA). The agreement established strict limits on Iran’s uranium enrichment, with a 3.67 percent cap, while expanding International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) monitoring and providing sanctions relief in exchange for nuclear restrictions.

The implementation of the JCPOA followed a phased process. First came the agreement in July 2015, followed by Adoption Day in October, then Implementation Day in January 2016 after the IAEA verified Iran’s initial nuclear commitments. Only after verification did major sanctions relief begin.

The lesson from this experience is not that agreements based on sequencing always fail. Rather, it is that sequencing without durable political guarantees is vulnerable.

When the US withdrew from the JCPOA in 2018 and restored sanctions, Iran concluded that technical commitments alone were insufficient. From the Iranian perspective, the central problem became the absence of guarantees that a future agreement would survive political changes in Washington.

The US, however, has its own concerns. US policymakers argue that sanctions relief must be linked to verifiable Iranian commitments, especially regarding the nuclear programme. They fear that providing economic benefits too early could reduce Washington’s leverage.

This is the strongest argument against synchronised steps: critics argue that deep mistrust makes simultaneous implementation unrealistic. They warn that Iran could use economic relief to rebuild its capabilities, while Washington worries that it could lose its negotiating advantage.

But the answer is not to abandon reciprocity. The answer is to design stronger verification mechanisms. A workable model would not rely on trust alone. It would rely on verification.

For example, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz could be linked to a phased easing of restrictions, with each stage monitored by a third party. Qatar, given its role as a mediator, could help facilitate communication, while technical nuclear issues could remain under international verification through the IAEA.

The principle would be simple: every Iranian action would have a clearly defined US response, and every US step would have a measurable Iranian obligation.

This approach is more realistic than demanding unilateral concessions because it gives both governments political space at home. Neither side would appear to be surrendering under pressure; both could argue that they are receiving something in return.

Recent diplomacy has already moved partially in this direction. The June memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran, supported by Qatar and other mediators, attempted to create mechanisms for reducing tensions, including issues related to military operations and freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. Later discussions included technical committees and monitoring mechanisms designed to manage implementation.

Qatar’s mediation has also become increasingly significant. Doha has attempted to bridge the gap between Tehran’s demand for confidence-building measures before negotiations and Washington’s insistence that nuclear issues remain central.

The recent message from US Vice President JD Vance to Iranian officials also reflected this dilemma. Washington signalled willingness to explore renewed negotiations, but insisted that the nuclear issue remain part of the discussion. Tehran, meanwhile, has continued to argue that pressure must be reduced before broader talks can succeed.

The question facing both capitals is therefore not whether compromise is possible. It is whether they can design a process in which compromise becomes politically survivable.

The Middle East has already paid a high price for the belief that pressure alone can produce strategic outcomes. Military escalation, economic disruption and energy uncertainty have demonstrated the limits of confrontation.

The next diplomatic test will not be whether Iran or the US is willing to make the first concession. It will be whether both sides are prepared to accept a more difficult but more practical formula: not trust before action, but verified action that gradually creates trust.

The future of Iran-US diplomacy may depend on replacing the politics of the first move with the discipline of the synchronised move.
