articles.title: 'Unfortunate': Govt condemns anti-India campaign by Chinese vloggers, urges Bangladesh to take action
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs on Tuesday condemned an alleged coordinated anti-India campaign by Chinese nationals who have reportedly been
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs on Tuesday condemned an alleged coordinated anti-India campaign by Chinese nationals who have reportedly been filming videos in slum areas of Dhaka for months and portraying the locations as parts of New Delhi during livestreams on Chinese social media platforms.During the weekly press briefing, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal termed the incident as "unfortunate" and said that attempts to project a distorted picture of a country only undermine the credibility of those involved and those backing them."We have seen media reports in this regard. Such efforts to present a distorted picture of any country are unfortunate," Jaiswal said."Insofar as efforts to buy foreign elements to portray Dhaka as Delhi are concerned, the peddling of false narratives only undermines the credibility of those who are undertaking such actions and those who are behind them. And I would urge the authorities concerned to take action against such people," he added.According to recent media reports, Chinese vloggers and livestreamers have been recording videos in impoverished neighbourhoods of Dhaka, Bangladesh, while falsely identifying the locations as parts of New Delhi.The videos reportedly feature derogatory remarks about India's living conditions, sanitation, food habits and poverty.According to Prothom Alo, the activity has been reported in Sector 12 of Uttara and the adjoining Tekpara area of Dhaka, where local residents estimate that more than 150 Chinese nationals have been recording videos.The vloggers reportedly walk through streets and alleyways carrying two mobile phones, livestreaming for hours and, at times, entering people's homes to film. Their activities, which have continued for months, have increasingly angered residents, who remain unaware of where the footage is being published and how it is being presented.A Chinese national identified as Fangyou told Prothom Alo that the livestreams were part of product promotion activities on WeChat. A Bangladeshi woman, Ritu Akhter, who works as a guide for the Chinese nationals, said they also earned money by posting videos on platforms such as Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok."This is New Delhi. Their homes are extremely dirty. There isn't even a fan inside the tin-roofed houses. This place is quite underdeveloped, dirty and unhygienic, and the law-and-order situation is poor," she said.Apart from the misleading portrayal of their neighbourhoods, residents have raised concerns over repeated filming and alleged intrusions into their homes. Some claimed that the Chinese nationals entered houses and even bathrooms while recording."Sometimes they enter our homes and start filming. We are not always properly dressed inside our houses. articles.title: Malaysian court clears former PM Najib Razak for house arrest transfer
articles.summary: Najib, 73, was jailed for his role in looting the now-defunct sovereign wealth fund 1MDB.
articles.body:
A Malaysian court has cleared the way for jailed former Prime Minister Najib Razak to be transferred to house arrest after an earlier directive was disputed.

“In accordance with the order of conditional pardon, the accused shall serve the remainder of the reduced sentence of six years’ imprisonment under house arrest,” Kuala Lumpur High Court Judge Aslam Zainuddin said on Tuesday.

Najib, 73, was jailed for his role in one of the largest thefts of public funds ever recorded from the now-defunct 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB) and was granted a conditional pardon in September.

On Friday, Najib’s political party paid the ⁠$12m fine as part of the terms of ⁠the royal pardon, and he was due to leave prison. However in a last-minute intervention, the attorney general postponed his transfer to house arrest after raising questions over the legal interpretation of the ⁠royal pardon and the court order allowing Najib to leave jail.

King Sultan Ibrahim has warned that any attempt to challenge his order to ‌let ‌Najib leave jail and move to house arrest could amount to defiance against his decree.

The king, a position held in rotation by Malaysia’s nine regional sultans, plays a largely ceremonial role but has the authority to grant pardons ‌under ‌discretionary powers granted by Malaysia’s Constitution.

Reporting from outside the court in Kuala Lumpur, Al Jazeera’s Rob McBride said: “This has caused all manner of political and constitutional controversy in Malaysia. The king made it plain he wasn’t happy with the interference of the attorney general over the weekend, and that it set a very difficult precedent.” He said it underlines the complicated, delicate relationship between the monarchy, the courts and the government.

The house arrest order applies only to Najib’s first conviction.

He faces ⁠an additional 15 years in prison after being found guilty last year in another 1MDB-linked case with the sentence set to begin after his stint under ⁠house arrest ends.

Najib has appealed the case, and his lawyers requested that the jail term and fines be halted, citing his poor health and inability to pay the fine.

articles.title: How did Mildenhall become crucial to the US Air Force?
articles.summary: RAF Mildenhall is the main European refuelling tanker base for US forces in Europe.
articles.body:
For 75 years there has been a slice of America on the outskirts of a small market town in Suffolk.

RAF Mildenhall began life as a base for British bombers throughout the 1930s and World War Two before becoming a hub for US operations in Europe in 1951.

Residents in west Suffolk are used to the sight and sounds of huge planes. RAF Lakenheath, also used by the US military, is just 5.5 miles (8.8km) away from Mildenhall.

On Monday, reports emerged that almost all aircraft had left RAF Mildenhall due to an alleged threat from Iran. But what is the significance of the base?

The base is on the outskirts of the market town of Mildenhall in Suffolk.

Although the site belongs to the Ministry of Defence (MoD), it is operated by the US Air Force (USAF).

About 3,000 military personnel are stationed at the base, which is about 80 miles (130km) north of London.

The USAF's other UK bases include RAF Lakenheath, also in Suffolk - home to the 48th Fighter Wing operating F-15 and F-35 jets - and RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, which regularly hosts deployments of long-range American aircraft.

RAF Fairford was the target of an alleged Iran-linked plot in September.

The MoD and US Air Force have not confirmed why aircraft were removed from RAF Mildenhall.

The base opened as an RAF bomber station in 1934 and played a key part in World War Two before the US Air Force moved onto the base in 1951.

The official opening by King George V in October 1934 coincided with the Royal Aero Club's England-to-Australia air race, which saw 20 aircraft race from Mildenhall to Melbourne.

Within six hours of the official declaration of war on Germany in 1939, bombers took off from RAF Mildenhall.

Throughout the rest of World War Two aircraft including Lancaster, Stirling and Wellington bombers flew from the base.

They were involved in crucial operations, including some of the first night bombings of Germany in 1940, raids on Cologne in 1942, the last major raid against Berlin and D-Day on 6 June 1944.

The US took over the base in 1951, operating B-29 and B-50 bombers.

During the 1990s it became the main European refuelling tanker base, operating Stratotankers.

The base is mostly used for refuelling and maintenance operations.

It is home to the 100th Air Refuelling Wing, the only permanent U.S. air refuelling wing in Europe.

Planes include KC-135 Stratotankers, the CV-22 Osprey, the RC-135V/W Rivet Joint reconnaissance aircraft and MC-130J Commando II, according to the RAF Mildenhall website .

It has been used as a staging area for aircraft and material bound for the Middle East.

Air refuelling tankers were "forward deployed" to the region during operations against Iran.

Flights carrying US presidents have often used RAF Mildenhall for refuelling, or as a base for Air Force One to land during visits to the UK.

Aviation enthusiasts are often outside the gates.

In 2024, drones were spotted over RAF Lakenheath, RAF Mildenhall and RAF Feltwell in Norfolk, sparking a major alert.

An investigation by The International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), a think-tank focusing on defence and security, said the "unmanned aerial vehicles" were likely launched from Russian-linked commercial vessels in the North Sea.

In 2020, the US Airforce reversed a decision that would have seen RAF Mildenhall shut in 2027.

The base was described as "crucial to operational efficiency" of US forces in Europe.

articles.title: Amber alert as Scotland faces blood donation shortages
articles.summary: An amber alert has been issued after stockpiles of blood fell below target several times in recent months
articles.body:
An amber alert has come into force for the first time as stocks of blood in Scotland have dropped to unprecedented low levels due to the shortage of donors.

The warning has been sent to hospitals across the country by the Scottish National Blood Transfusion Service (SNBTS), urging medical staff to only use Type O blood when essential.

Type O blood is particularly important for transfusions as O-negative acts as a universal donor and O-positive is the most common blood type in the UK, with about 35% of the population having it.

Stocks have consistently been below target levels for several weeks and Group O blood has fallen to below two days of reserves on several occasions recently.

SNBTS aims to always retain 5 – 7 days supply of all blood groups.

The alert comes after a decline in people joining the blood donation register.

In the past decade SNBTS said there had been a 24% drop in blood donors - about 30,000 people.

The blood transfusion service said it was particularly struggling to attract younger donors.

Hospitals are estimated to need about 135,000 units of blood each year to treat patients.

The SNBTS said that to do this appointments at its five national donor centres in Aberdeen, Dundee, Edinburgh, Glasgow and Inverness needed to be fully booked all year round.

However, an average of just 85% of these appointment slots are filled.

Debbie McNaughton, director of donor and transport services at the SNBTS, told Radio Scotland Breakfast that currently, about 2% of Scotland's population are signed up to give blood, with the majority donating once a year.

"If they could be donating maybe twice or three times a year, that would hugely help to provide resilience for the blood supply," she said.

McNaughton went on to urge anyone who is healthy and 17 or over to sign up to the donor register.

The amber alert will trigger new protocols in hospitals to minimise non-essential usage of O-type blood, but emergency operations, blood transfusions, transplants and cancer surgeries will continue as normal.

The alert has initially been issued for an initial period of 4-6 weeks but will be kept under close review.

articles.title: Met Police investigate several reports on Russell Brand following his conviction
articles.summary: Det Supt Andy Furphy says the force had received "several reports in during the trial and since the trial".
articles.body:
The officer who led the investigation into Russell Brand has said that the Metropolitan Police have received "several reports during the trial and since the trial" following the disgraced comedian's conviction and sentence.

Speaking to BBC Breakfast on Tuesday, Det Supt Andy Furphy said that officers were in the "process of triaging" those reports and were "looking at exactly what we've got, whether they're information that points to behaviour or whether they could constitute a criminal offence, so our work isn't done."

Brand is already being investigated over rape allegations from two more women. He has been interviewed under caution in connection to those allegations.

On Monday, he was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison, after being convicted of rape and sexual assault.

In his sentencing remarks, judge Joel Bennathan described Brand as a "sexual predator" and criticised his "staggering arrogance".

The 51-year-old was sentenced to nine years for rape, with an additional 18 months, nine months and eight months for three counts of sexual assault. The latter sentences are to run concurrently.

He was found guilty of the charges involving four women between 2004 and 2009.

Asked by BBC Breakfast how the women in the case who gave evidence in the trial were coping, Furphy said: "Some have found it deeply distressing because of the amount of media attention wrapped around it".

"Even Russell Brand himself before and during trial was putting material online, but we continue to support them."

Furphy noted how the conviction "could not have been achieved" without their "bravery, their courage, their resilience throughout the whole criminal justice process".

He continued: "It's deeply personal and quite harrowing to be a victim of rape and sexual assault, and to have to tell anybody about it, let alone police officers.

"But I'm glad they did. I'm glad they put their trust in us."

A Met spokesperson confirmed that "several people have contacted the investigation team during and since the trial to provide information or report a potential criminal allegation".

They added that "detectives are assessing this information as part of their ongoing enquiries".

MP Dame Caroline Dinenage has re-iterated her concerns about the fact Brand was able to post videos online in the build-up to and during his trial to his millions of followers.

"This does continue to be an issue that he has made money throughout the process on his social media platform," she told BBC Breakfast.

"It just felt very odd that during the height of when there was a police investigation and some really serious allegations in the paper, that he was able to go online to his two and a half million followers, denying everything and putting his side of the story forward.

"That was an opportunity that his victims didn't have."

In September 2023, after the Sunday Times and Channel 4 Dispatches allegations were made against Brand, Culture, Media and Sport (CMS) Committee chair Dame Caroline wrote to social media companies Rumble, X, TikTok and Meta.

She asked if they would follow YouTube in cutting off Brand's income on their platforms. Rumble publicly refused, and X said it does not take action against accounts that have not broken its rules or the law. TikTok said he had never been monetised there.

"We know that he had used his following [online] to try and cow people into silence," added Dame Caroline.

"And the fact that they [the women] were able to come forward and tell their story and tell their truth and secure this conviction because of it is unbelievably impressive."

articles.title: Trump says Israel, Gulf allies must repay Iran war cost: What does it mean?
articles.summary: Analysts say Trump’s comments are more likely to be political posturing than a reflection of serious policy priorities.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has said the US plans to seek compensation from countries it “protected” during its war on Iran.

In an interview with CBS News correspondent Ross Douthat that aired Sunday, Trump said such countries would “pay us any and all costs we had for the war”.

“We’re going to get all that money back,” Trump said. “They’re going to do it, 100 percent. Because without us, they wouldn’t exist.”

For the first time, Trump also explicitly spoke of compensation from Israel, which he said “wouldn’t exist” without US military intervention.

The reimbursement demand comes after Trump and his Republican party took a drubbing in midterm elections, which the president has conceded was partly due to public discontent over the Iran war.

The US president has since declared the war “effectively over” militarily , while defending his decision to start the conflict as “a very good decision”.

Here’s what to know about Trump’s demand for repayment, and what it could mean for the US and its allies:

Which countries does Trump want compensation from?

Trump — for the first time — singled out Israel, which was a direct participant in the war against Iran from the outset.

“We decapitated their [Iran’s] nuclear arsenal,” he said. “If I didn’t do that, there would be no Israel right now. Israel would be gone.”

Previously, Trump has said he would seek repayment from Gulf countries that benefit from the US military presence around the embattled Strait of Hormuz, where US forces have been escorting vessels .

“We’re protecting a very rich portion of the world, we’re spending money, and so what we’ve done is we’re going to be reimbursed for protection,” Trump said during a press briefing in July.

He named Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain and Kuwait as countries that should pay.

But while Israel jointly launched the war on Iran with the US, Gulf countries have said that they were not even informed about Washington’s plans, and have since borne the brunt of Iran’s retaliatory attacks. As members of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), they have called for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict.

$47.1bn as of mid-October, according to the US military .

But the full cost is likely to be even higher, as that figure excludes the cost of repairing damage to US military bases across the Middle East.

The Congressional Budget Office in September estimated the conflict would carry an additional cost of $2bn-$3bn for each month it continues.

Will Trump actually seek repayment from allies?

Neil Quilliam, an associate fellow at Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa Programme, told Al Jazeera that Trump’s comments are “best understood as political signalling rather than a serious policy proposal.”

Gulf states in particular are likely to take Trump’s comments “with a grain of salt,” added Bader al-Saif, an assistant professor of history at Kuwait University and associate fellow at Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa programme.

“I think what [Trump] stated on an American news channel was for domestic consumption, and I think that’s how most of the Gulf states will take it,” said al-Saif.

Stefan Lukas, an analyst specialising in Middle East and North Africa security and foreign policy, also pointed to Trump’s domestic political considerations, saying the US president has been “looking for someone to blame … and has been doing everything in his power to divert attention from the midterm election results”.

Lukas told Al Jazeera it is unlikely that Washington’s Arab allies in the region will face large compensation payments “or anything similar”.

However, he suggested that Trump could be more serious about seeking economic concessions from Israel, particularly after announcing that the country would no longer receive US aid after the end of this year.

That is partly because, from Trump’s perspective, “Israel pushed him into a disastrous war with Iran”, Lukas said.

Al-Saif said Trump could be “very innovative” in defining what constitutes repayment for the war, potentially pointing to existing trade agreements or investment from the Gulf.

“There’s many agreements for him to go back to and to claim,” said Al-Saif. “There have been a lot of [Gulf] pledges for investment in the US.”

Farid Boussaid, an assistant professor in Middle East politics at the University of Amsterdam, said Washington could push for further Gulf investment and present it as compensation.

“This will most likely be indirect and take the form of commercial investments in the US, buying of US weapons systems – on top of what has already been ordered – and investments into close associates of Trump’s financial dealings,” said Boussaid.

Trump has repeatedly made misleading claims about foreign investment and trade agreements in the past, portraying them as payments or gifts to the US.

After a July 2025 trade deal with the European Union , Trump claimed the bloc had given the US a $600bn “gift” that could be invested in “anything we want”. However, the framework agreement referred only to an expectation that European companies would invest $600bn across strategic sectors in the US through 2028.

The same month, Trump described a $550bn investment pledge from Japan, under a new US-Japan trade agreement, as being “like a signing bonus that a baseball player would get”.

During Trump’s first term, he repeatedly claimed that Mexico would pay for a border wall – which was never completed and which Mexico did not pay for. Trump later qualified his claim to say that Mexico would reimburse the US for the wall or pay for a “piece” of it, which also never happened. Trump at one point claimed that the benefits of a trade pact he negotiated with Mexico would cover the cost of the wall.

How will US allies react to Trump’s demands?

Having already suffered extensive financial losses during the war, the US’s Gulf allies will not take well to being asked to pay more for a war they did not start, say analysts.

Quilliam said Gulf leaders would likely respond to any demand for direct repayment with “quiet resistance”, arguing that they “already contribute significantly to the cost of regional security through defence cooperation, investment and economic partnerships with the US”.

Gulf states also pay for the maintenance of several large bases that the US uses for military operations in the region.

Boussaid said Gulf states will be particularly averse to such a demand as “the US-Israeli war led to considerable damage to their [civilian] and military infrastructure when Iran struck back”.

Al-Saif added that Trump’s “condescending language does not bode well for partners long invested in the relationship with the US”.

As for Israel, it looks unlikely to “reverse its longstanding role as a recipient rather than a provider of support in its relationship with the US”, according to Marzieh Kouhi Esfahani, assistant professor of politics and international relations of the Middle East at Durham University.

“While Israel and the United States continue to share intelligence and coordinate on regional security issues, any request for Israel to shoulder a meaningful share of the financial burden would run against established practice and Israel’s present resource constraints,” she said.

articles.title: PAUL MAURO: Sanctuary states have a DMV problem — and Trump can demand answers
articles.summary: Donald Trump's DOT withheld $73 million from New York after an audit found over half of commercial trucking licenses went to illegal drivers.
articles.body: The Democrats have captured both houses of Congress and are gleefully announcing, "woke is back." But there’s one inconvenient detail: President Donald Trump still controls the executive branch. Why does that matter? Because Ryan O’Shea mattered. ICE LODGES DETAINER FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED IN WRONG-WAY MARYLAND CRASH THAT KILLED MOM, DAUGHTER On October 16, 21-year-old Ryan O’Shea, a University of New Haven hockey captain studying criminal justice, was driving home from a game when a pickup truck traveling the wrong way on Connecticut’s Interstate 91 slammed head-on into his car. Ryan was killed instantly. Police say the other driver was Guillermo Carmona-Lopez, who is a Mexican national who DHS says had already been removed from the United States twice. Somehow, he was back. ILLEGAL ALIEN'S ‘INEXCUSABLE’ CRIME SPARKS INTERSTATE CLASH BETWEEN GOP SEN, DEM GOV: ‘YOU SHOULD BE ASHAMED’ The story circulated widely on social media, but received limited mainstream coverage. One needn’t wonder why. Ryan was not a member of any of our media’s preferred victim classes, he wanted to go into law enforcement, and he was allegedly killed by someone who the feds say shouldn’t have been here. Three strikes. But his death raises a larger question: How is it possible that so many foreign drivers are permitted — or even assisted — in getting licensed to drive on our roads? Is there more going on here? Examples similar to Ryan’s are legion. In July, Uzbek national Bekhzod Asrarov, who had entered the U.S. legally, allegedly killed 21-year-old college soccer player Tobias "Toby" Forsythe when his tractor-trailer slammed into the young man’s car. Asrarov, who held an Ohio CDL, reportedly couldn’t communicate with police without Google Translate, failed an English-proficiency test and allegedly attempted to conceal evidence, including his electronic driving logs. Then, on September 2, Indian national Manjit Singh, whom DHS identified as illegal, was involved in another fatal Ohio crash that killed 50-year-old Brenda Watson. Singh held a California CDL and has been charged with aggravated vehicular homicide. We could go on. Ohio has at least moved to tighten the loopholes that allowed this. Too late for two Americans. TRUMP PROMOTES FREEDOM HAULERS INITIATIVE TO FAST-TRACK MILITARY VETERANS INTO TRUCKING JOBS But that’s more than blue states are willing to do. So in September 2025, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced emergency restrictions on CDLs issued to foreign drivers after a nationwide audit uncovered widespread fraud. In New York alone, Duffy’s audit found that over half of commercial trucking licenses went to illegal drivers — and those drivers hit the roads across the country. In one case, investigators found that a Chinese national accused of causing a fatal highway pileup in Tennessee was illegally issued a New York State driver’s license. In California, the audit found that 25% of CDLs were unlawfully issued — with a stated policy that California will not enforce federal English proficiency rules. So this year, Duffy began the process of cracking down on the practice nationwide. He withheld $73 million from New York State, which refuses to comply (and is suing in response). But more significantly, the feds announced "Joint Task Force Crossroads of America," a nationwide initiative targeting fraud and criminal activity regarding CDLs. DEADLY ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT TRUCK CRASH EXPOSED FAILURES ON THE ROAD AND AT THE BORDER: KEY SENATOR How widespread is the problem? The task force started with more than 1,000 leads and inspected more than 200 driving schools across 23 states. Multiple criminal investigations have already been opened. It’s a start. But let’s recall: Guillermo Carmona-Lopez, who allegedly killed Ryan O’Shea, did not have a CDL. DOJ ESCALATES BLUE-STATE ICE STANDOFF AFTER STATES REFUSE KEY FEDERAL REQUEST So limiting the task force to just CDL enforcement is a mistake. articles.title: 'SNL' writer’s sister vanished — now her boyfriend and rival face charges in deadly love triangle
articles.summary: "Saturday Night Live" writer Jimmy Fowlie's sister Christina Downer faced alleged stalking and blackmail before her disappearance and presumed death.
articles.body: Months before a "Saturday Night Live" writer's sister disappeared, court records showed a pattern of alleged stalking, threats, and domestic violence involving two suspects now charged with her death and disappearance. Last month, Los Angeles County prosecutors charged Christina Downer’s boyfriend, Delorean Bijon Brandon, 41, with first-degree murder. Brandon’s former girlfriend, Kaylee Nicole Markowski, 34, is facing two felony counts of being an accessory after the fact. Investigators believe Brandon killed Downer, 38, on or around Sept. 19, 2025. Her remains have not been located. Before Downer disappeared, she and Brandon sought separate restraining orders against Markowski, accusing her, in part, of stalking and blackmail, court records showed. Both cases were dismissed after Downer and Brandon failed to appear in court, according to court documents obtained by Los Angeles Magazine. 'SNL' WRITER'S MISSING SISTER CASE LEADS HOMICIDE DETECTIVES TO JOSHUA TREE MONTHS AFTER FAMILY'S MURDER CLAIM Downer’s disappearance and presumed death Authorities learned of Downer’s disappearance in December 2025, when her ex-husband reported her missing, saying he had not heard from her in months. Downer’s brother, "Saturday Night Live" writer Jimmy Fowlie, began posting public pleas on Instagram that same month, asking for information about his sister’s whereabouts. Brandon, who shared an apartment with Downer in Koreatown, told police that she had moved out months prior, leaving her belongings behind, including her car and beloved miniature pinscher named Rex. TEACHER FOUND DEAD WITH THROAT SLIT; DETECTIVES SCRUTINIZE HUSBAND’S SHIFTING STORY The LAPD’s Robbery-Homicide Division took over the investigation after Downer’s cellphone washed ashore at Santa Monica Beach. Investigators believe Brandon and Markowski used Downer’s phone to send messages, fabricating a story that she voluntarily disappeared, according to court documents. HORSE FARM OWNER GETS LIFE IN PRISON FOR BOYFRIEND'S MURDER AFTER CLAIMING SELF-DEFENSE "The individual(s) in possession of her phone used it to hide the fact she was gone, to ask for money, and to create a false narrative that she was going ‘off the grid,’" Fowlie wrote on Instagram in April. "I am sharing this because I believe that whoever is responsible is hoping to erase her in every way possible. I want to amplify her story in the only way I know how. And express that she was a beautiful person who matters in this world, especially to me." Fowlie did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Restraining orders, prior domestic violence allegations In a September 2024 restraining order petition obtained by the Los Angeles Times, Downer accused Markowski of terrorizing her since December 2023. Markowski harassed Downer by threatening to break into her home, beat her up and by calling her racial slurs, court documents stated. She also allegedly stole Downer’s cat and a storage device containing intimate videos, which she allegedly used to blackmail Downer. "She calls us n-----, threatens to beat me up, stole my spare key and copied it, threatens to break into my home," Downer claimed in her request. 'HOW I MET YOUR MOTHER' ACTOR NICK PASQUAL CONVICTED OF ATTEMPTED MURDER FOR STABBING EX-GIRLFRIEND In July 2025, Brandon filed a domestic violence restraining order request against Markowski, alleging she harassed him, targeted his vehicle and attempted to interfere with Downer’s job, according to ABC7’s court records review. Judges dismissed both cases after Downer and Brandon failed to appear in court. In September 2025, Brandon sought another protective order against Markowski, accusing her of hitting and kicking him when he tried to leave. He said she also threatened to shoot him in the head for having a relationship with Downer. A Los Angeles County Superior Court judge rejected the request and set a Sept. 23, 2025, hearing. Alyce LaViolette, a licensed marriage and family therapist and domestic violence specialist not affiliated with the case, explained that courts usually examine specific details of each allegation rather than the number of complaints filed before deciding if a case proceeds. Court backlogs and limited domestic violence training can make it more difficult to assess a full abuse history, she said. On Sept. 18, 2025, however, Brandon withdrew the request. Investigators believe Downer died within a day of Brandon withdrawing the request. Previous accusations The latest criminal complaint detailed allegations of domestic violence carried out by Brandon against a different woman. Brandon allegedly used scissors during one of the assaults, according to documents obtained by Los Angeles Magazine. He is now charged with two felony counts of injuring a cohabitant in connection with the alleged 2022 assaults. In a separate April 2022 court case, a woman filed a civil harassment restraining order petition against Markowski in Los Angeles County Superior Court. The judge dismissed the case in June 2022 for "lack of prosecution." FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X Greg Risling, an executive assistant at the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office, declined to comment on an open case, directing Fox News Digital to a previous release. Markowski’s attorney, Arvand Naderi, also declined to comment on a pending case. Risling said Brandon is being represented by the Alternate Public Defender’s Office. articles.title: Before the next catastrophe strikes: India’s armed forces gear up for mega disaster response drill
articles.summary: India's armed forces are often among the first to respond when disaster strikes, both at home and abroad.
articles.body: India's armed forces are often among the first to respond when disaster strikes, both at home and abroad. Ensuring that the Army, Navy, Air Force and other agencies can work together seamlessly is the objective of the Annual Joint Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief Exercise 2026 (AJHE-26), scheduled to be held at Air Force Station Jamnagar from November 17 to 19.The exercise will bring together the three services, the Indian Coast Guard, disaster management authorities and representatives of friendly foreign countries. The National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), state disaster management authorities (SDMAs) and other agencies will also participate.The focus will be on strengthening inter-agency coordination, improving operational interoperability and developing international response mechanisms for emergencies such as cyclones, earthquakes, floods and chemical disasters. AJHE-26 will comprise a table-top exercise, alongside a demonstration of capabilities for participating officials and representatives.Discussions will centre on the roles and responsibilities of different agencies, standard operating procedures (SOPs) for disaster response and the coordination required to mobilise personnel and equipment. Participants will also assess the air assets and other resources that the armed forces and civilian agencies can bring to relief operations. The Indian Air Force's Rapid Action Medical Team will demonstrate the role of military medical units in responding to emergencies.The broader objective is to harmonise response procedures and establish a common understanding among all participating agencies, including international partners, so that assistance can be mobilised and delivered more quickly when a major disaster strikes. Bringing together the armed forces, the Coast Guard, central and state authorities and foreign representatives reflects a whole-of-nation approach to disaster response while strengthening India's ability to coordinate humanitarian assistance with international partners.A record as a first responderIndia has built a considerable track record as a first responder, deploying aircraft, ships, medical teams and specialised personnel to disaster-hit regions both within the country and overseas.The latest example is the Indian Air Force's deployment of a C-130 aircraft carrying 10 tonnes of relief material and medical supplies to Nepal following flash floods, with further assistance planned through C-17 aircraft.India's record of humanitarian assistance stretches back decades, from the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami to Operation Cactus in 1988, when Indian forces helped the Maldives thwart an attempted coup. More recent operations include Operation Amistad in Venezuela, where two IAF C-17 aircraft transported an Army field hospital and more than 35 tonnes of supplies following an earthquake in June. In 2025, India launched Operation Sagar Bandhu in Sri Lanka and Operation Brahma in Myanmar. Other major missions include Operation Dost in Turkey and Syria, Operation Kaveri in Sudan and Operation Karuna in Myanmar, all undertaken in 2023.The armed forces have also played a crucial role in evacuating Indians from conflict zones and crisis-hit regions. Operation Ganga brought back more than 20,000 Indians from Ukraine in 2022, while Operation Devi Shakti evacuated Indian citizens and officials from Afghanistan in 2021. Earlier missions include Samudra Setu, Raahat, Maitri, Sankat Mochan and Neer.These operations demonstrate India's ability to rapidly deploy military assets, medical facilities and specialised teams across the region and beyond. AJHE-26 seeks to strengthen the coordination that makes such responses possible.

articles.title: Grand Theatre Blackpool's £300k renovation offers comfier seats
articles.summary: The Grade II* listed theatre revamp improves facilities for audiences in the top gallery tier.
articles.body:
A much-loved Victorian theatre has said the £300,000 transformation of its top gallery tier would provide audiences with "21st Century comfort".

Designed by Frank Matcham - one of Britain's most renowned theatre architects - the Grade II* listed Grand Theatre Blackpool was built in 1894.

The renovation project has seen 301 original wooden bench seats replaced with 216 individual seats - each with a back and armrests - as well as improved accessibility and the restoration after 10 years of the gallery bar.

Adam Knight, the theatre's chief executive, said the revamp would give audiences "a much more comfortable experience while bringing a long-neglected part of the theatre back to life".

The National Lottery Heritage Fund provided £250,000 towards the project, which is the second phase of the theatre's major refurbishment .

The Friends of the Grand have contributed the remaining £50,000.

The completion of the renovation work marks the long-awaited ambition to improve the gallery, which accounts for almost a third of the theatre's seating.

During the auditorium restoration in 2002, plans to improve the gallery were unable to go ahead due to a lack of funding.

A temporary solution was introduced, with cushioned pads added to the original wooden benches.

They remained in place for more than two decades, though, offering cramped seating without backs or armrests and making the gallery an increasingly unpopular choice for modern audiences.

Knight said: "We're delighted to have completed this important refurbishment, giving audiences a much more comfortable experience while bringing a long-neglected part of the theatre back to life.

"We've been careful to preserve the heritage and original character of Frank Matcham's design, while reusing materials wherever possible."

Original tiering, handrails and sightlines have been restored, while carpets have been removed to reveal the floorboards beneath, which have been stained and varnished to reflect their original appearance.

Alongside the seating improvements, the auditorium stairs have been rebuilt to reflect the reduced number of seating tiers, while walkways have been widened to meet current safety standards.

Demountable seating has also been installed in the slips, which can be removed to create wheelchair spaces when lift access becomes available as part of a future phase of the theatre's wider renovation.

Environmental considerations have been built into the refurbishment, with original materials being retained and repurposed.

The gallery's original floorboards have been used as kickboards and the countertop in the refurbished gallery bar.

Helen Featherstone, from the National Lottery Heritage Fund, said: "We're thrilled that thanks to National Lottery players, the Grade II* listed Blackpool Grand Theatre can now offer audiences a more comfortable experience while showcasing the stunning Matcham architecture and heritage details."

The next phase of the masterplan will focus on incorporating the row of shops along the Church Street side of the theatre and creating a new cafe-bar, with lift access to all levels of the auditorium and further accessibility improvements.

articles.title: The last arc of poverty: Why India’s next big battle runs from UP to Bengal
articles.summary: Explore how India is making significant strides in reducing poverty, focusing on the regions from Uttar Pradesh to West Bengal, and the challenges that remain as millions strive for economic stability.
articles.body: India’s sharp decline in extreme poverty has given the government much to celebrate. Prime Minister Narendra Modi hailed the World Bank’s latest findings as “A historic fall in poverty. A generational rise in opportunity.” He has linked the reduction in poverty to economic growth, infrastructure investment, welfare schemes and employment opportunities.The improvements are tangible. In 2011–12, roughly 27 out of every 100 Indians lived below the international extreme-poverty line of $3 a day. By 2023–24, fewer than three did. That is one of the fastest declines in poverty anywhere in the world. Yet the numbers reveal another, less discussed reality. About 57% of India’s poor live in a contiguous belt stretching from Uttar Pradesh to West Bengal, according to the World Bank’s October 2026 Poverty & Equity Brief.Globally, progress against extreme poverty has largely stalled. An estimated 81.1 crore people, or one in ten worldwide, live below $3 a day in 2026, virtually the same share as in 2019. Nearly 370 crore people, almost half the world’s population, live below the higher $8.30-a-day line. Slower growth, conflict and too few productive jobs have made further progress difficult.By comparison, India has made rapid progress. But the poverty that remains is concentrated in particular regions, and among households with fewer assets, less education and little access to stable, well-paying work. Further progress will increasingly depend on whether the states where poverty is concentrated can create better jobs and opportunities.The millions caught between poverty linesExtreme poverty, measured at $3 per person per day, fell from 27.1% in 2011–12 to 2.6% in 2023–24. At the higher $4.20-a-day line, which the World Bank uses for lower-middle-income countries such as India, poverty fell from 57.7% to 16.1%. The Bank estimates that the number of people below this line dropped by 49.6 crore over the period. Both lines are international consumption benchmarks, set in 2021 purchasing-power-parity (PPP) dollars, which adjust for what money buys in each country.In 2023–24, about 3.7 crore Indians were below the extreme-poverty line. About 23.3 crore were living below $4.20 a day. That leaves roughly 19.6 crore Indians above the extreme-poverty threshold but still below the higher line.Poverty rate and absolute numbersJharkhand had the highest extreme-poverty rate among Indian states in 2023–24, at about 12.9%, according to the World Bank’s September 2026 Subnational Poverty and Inequality Database. Bihar’s rate was much lower, at 4.1%.In absolute numbers, however, the two states are almost level. TOI combined the World Bank’s state poverty rates with Health Ministry population projections. By that estimate, Bihar had about 51.8 lakh people below the $3 line, and Jharkhand 51 lakh.Uttar Pradesh provides another example. Its extreme-poverty rate was about 2%, but its population is so large that nearly 47 lakh people were still estimated to be below the line. At the higher $4.20 line, Jharkhand’s poverty rate was 41.2%, compared with 21.6% in Bihar, 20.1% in Uttar Pradesh and 14.5% in West Bengal.Yet Uttar Pradesh, at less than half Jharkhand’s rate, had the largest number of people below this line among the four states, about 4.73 crore. Bihar had another 2.74 crore, Jharkhand 1.63 crore and West Bengal 1.44 crore.Together, these four states were home to about 10.54 crore people below $4.20 a day, by TOI’s calculations. That is nearly 47% of the total when the estimates for every state and Union territory are added up. But large numbers of poor people are not confined to the northern and eastern belt.Maharashtra, one of India’s largest state economies, had an estimated 2.34 crore people below $4.20 a day, the third-highest state total after Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. Its poverty rate at this threshold was 18.5%, lower than those of Bihar and Jharkhand, but its large population pushed the absolute number much higher. Even at the $3 extreme-poverty line, Maharashtra had an estimated 40 lakh people below the threshold, the fourth-largest number among states.Other measures show the same divideIndia’s own data on multidimensional poverty point the same way. NITI Aayog’s National Multidimensional Poverty Index measures deprivation across health, education and living standards rather than spending alone.Its survey-based findings show that Bihar’s multidimensional poverty rate fell from 51.9% in 2015–16 to 33.8% in 2019–21. Jharkhand’s declined from 42.1% to 28.8%, and Uttar Pradesh’s from 37.7% to 22.9%. Even after these falls, about one in three people in Bihar was still poor on this measure at the time of the survey.In 2023–24, average monthly spending per person in rural Jharkhand was ₹2,946, against a national rural average of ₹4,122, according to the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation’s household consumption survey. That is about 29% lower than the national rural average. The same survey found that people in Jharkhand’s towns and cities spent 83% more on average than those in its villages, the widest urban-rural gap among India’s 18 major states.More jobs, flat earningsEmployment has been a big driver of India’s fall in poverty. The World Bank estimates that the number of employed people rose by about 13.4 crore between 2017 and 2023, much of it driven by rural women entering work. An extra earner in a household can increase what the family spends and help it move above the poverty line. But the Bank notes that earnings, adjusted for inflation, stayed broadly unchanged, and much of the new employment was in relatively low-productivity work.According to the Periodic Labour Force Survey Annual Report 2025, 56.2% of employed Indians were self-employed, while 23.6% had regular wage or salaried jobs. Agriculture still accounted for 43% of employment. The share of regular salaried workers did rise, from 22.4% in 2024 to 23.6%, while agriculture’s share of employment fell.The government’s 2023–24 consumption survey found that average monthly spending per person was ₹3,652 in rural households dependent on casual farm labour, compared with ₹5,005 in rural households relying on regular salaried jobs outside farming. These figures measure household spending, not individual wages, but they show how much living standards vary with the type of work.Why moving out of farming may not be enoughLeaving farming does not automatically raise incomes, as Bihar shows. Services make up 58.7% of Bihar’s economic output, measured as gross value added, even though the state’s income per person is relatively low, according to the Union government’s Economic Survey 2025–26. But the survey notes that much of this output comes from low-value activities. By contrast, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu and Telangana together account for nearly 40% of India’s services output, supported by activities such as information technology, finance and professional services.A worker who leaves the fields for small-scale trading or another low-paying service job has moved into services too. But that does not necessarily bring the jump in earnings that a move into a more productive industry would. These states need jobs that pay better and offer a way up.Poverty’s effects can last beyond the poverty lineHousehold spending data also miss some consequences of deprivation, such as poor child nutrition. The latest National Family Health Survey, NFHS-6, conducted in 2023–24, shows that child nutrition has improved substantially across India. The share of children under five who are stunted, or too short for their age, fell nationally from 35.5% in 2019–21 to 29.3%.All four states at the centre of this analysis improved too. Stunting declined from 42.9% to 35.6% in Bihar, from 39.6% to 35% in Jharkhand, from 39.7% to 31.5% in Uttar Pradesh and from 33.8% to 22.4% in West Bengal.But a fall in stunting has not always come with a fall in the share of underweight children.In Jharkhand, the share of children under five who were underweight, or too light for their age, rose from 39.4% to 41.1%, even as stunting declined. In Uttar Pradesh, the underweight share also rose, from 32.1% to 34.5%. Bihar improved on both counts, with the underweight share falling from 41% to 35.7%. So did West Bengal, where it fell from 32.2% to 28.5%.Why the next phase could be harderSo far, India’s progress against poverty has been driven by rising consumption, more people in work and expanded government assistance, including food subsidies. The people still below the line may be harder to reach. As poverty falls, those who remain poor are increasingly concentrated in households with fewer assets, less education, more dependants and little access to stable employment.A young person growing up in a poorer district may have better chances at an education than their parents had, but no guarantee of a well-paying job nearby. The World Bank expects poverty to keep falling, though more slowly. Its projections suggest that the share of Indians below $4.20 a day will fall from 14.2% in 2026 to 12.1% in 2028.Living standards have improved across most states, including those in the northern and eastern belt. It is less clear whether growth can create more productive jobs and higher earnings in the places where a large share of poor households still live. Better infrastructure, education and healthcare will help. But households also need to be able to turn those gains into reliable incomes. India has already shown that poverty can fall sharply in just over a decade.The next phase will depend not only on lifting those still in extreme poverty, but also on what happens to the 19.6 crore Indians between the two poverty lines, who are above the lowest threshold but have yet to achieve economic security.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Fire breaks out outside electronic showroom in Patna
articles.summary: Fire outside electronic showroom near Patna’s Dak Bungalow Square triggers panic; blaze likely from short circuit, contained quickly with no injuries reported.
articles.body: Patna: A fire broke out outside an electronic showroom near Patna’s busy Dak Bungalow Square on Tuesday morning, triggering panic among shopkeepers and residents. A suspected short circuit is believed to have caused the blaze.The fire started in the lower portion of the Grand Plaza building and spread upwards after banners and posters outside the showroom caught fire. Thick smoke soon engulfed the premises, prompting people in nearby shops to rush out.Local shopkeepers and residents initially tried to douse the flames before fire brigade teams arrived and launched an operation. Firefighters faced difficulties due to thick smoke and combustible materials but eventually brought the blaze under control.District fire officer Abhishek Kumar said the building housed an electronic showroom dealing in refrigerators, washing machines and other gadgets. The flames spread through the poster hoarding outside the shop but did not reach its interiors. The fire was contained before entering the showroom, and no one was injured.According to the fire department, two MT Mist Technology vehicles, four water tenders, a water bowser, a rescue tender and one hydraulic lift were deployed to tackle the blaze.Preliminary findings suggested that a short circuit triggered the fire. As the flames remained largely confined to the exterior, extensive damage to the goods stored inside the showroom was avoided.
